Brief Intelligence

A clearer way into EU case law.

Our team built a legal research tool for Professor Maria Amparo Grau Ruiz. It brings more than 20,000 Court of Justice of the European Union cases into a searchable interface with topic and year filters, ranked results, and case details.

The project

Legal researchers need ways to find cases by substance, not just by a known citation. We built Brief Intelligence for Professor Maria Amparo Grau Ruiz, a Visiting Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

Our team combined an EU case collection, automated classification, and a web interface so researchers could search, narrow, and inspect relevant decisions. The project was a team prototype and demo; this page does not claim deployment or adoption by the law school.

My role
Search experience and results interface
Team
Adi Rosenstock, Clark Hanlon, and Zachary Braffman
Scope
20,000+ EU court cases

From case collection to useful result

Prepare the corpus

The team pipeline gathered EU case metadata, classified legal topics, and prepared abstracts and source links for search.

Search and narrow

The interface searches titles, CELEX identifiers, and abstracts. Topic, year, and US relevance filters help researchers refine a broad question.

Inspect the source

Ranked results lead to case details and EUR-Lex links, so a researcher can move from a promising match to the underlying decision.

My contribution

I worked on the React search experience and results interface. My commits added Lunr.js indexing, query expansion, search history and autocomplete, exact phrase handling, sorting, date boosts, and refinements to the results table and page layout.

Clark Hanlon also worked extensively on the app and its case summary features. Zachary Braffman built the public data and classification pipeline. Brief Intelligence was a shared project, and the corpus and application were team outputs.

A key decision

Keep the search responsive and the source visible.

The team classified cases before search. The interface then used a client-side index and explicit ranking rules to retrieve results without waiting for a model on every query. Case details point back to EUR-Lex so the researcher can check the primary source.
